title: The Colorado River Compact
summary: Josh and Chuck explain the Colorado River Compact of 1922, signed in Santa Fe, New Mexico, which divided the river's water between the upper and lower basin states. They cover the prior appropriation doctrine, Herbert Hoover's role, the split at Lee Ferry, the flawed flow estimate (16.4 million acre feet, with the LaRue study ignored), the Law of the River (Boulder Canyon Project Act, Arizona v. California, Colorado River Basin Project Act, Central Arizona Project, Endangered Species Act, salinity control with Mexico), the 2000-2023 drought, Lake Powell and Lake Mead concerns, agriculture and cattle use, the 2024 basin state proposals and stalemate, and the federal report in January 2026. The episode ends with a listener mail segment about capri pants.
topics: cattle ranching and alfalfa water use

segments.title: Opening and Colorado River overview
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the Colorado River Compact, a listener suggestion, and the river's importance to seven states and Mexico, with the basin states' shared water sharing.

segments.title: Why water matters and the Hoover and Imperial Dams
segments.summary: The desert climate and low rainfall make the river vital. Dams such as Hoover and Imperial help bank water, and the upper basin fills those banks.

segments.title: Prior appropriation and the 1922 compact origins
segments.summary: A Supreme Court decision applying prior appropriation across state lines alarmed upstream states. Seven states negotiated the compact in Santa Fe in November 1922.

segments.title: Herbert Hoover's role and the compact negotiations
segments.summary: Herbert Hoover, Secretary of Commerce, proposed splitting the river into two halves. The New Mexico representative voted yes reluctantly. The negotiators met 27 times.

segments.title: Lee Ferry dividing point
segments.summary: Lee Ferry, on the border between upper and lower basins, is where the river is measured. It is not the same as the Lee's Ferry near the Grand Canyon.

segments.title: Water volumes, acre feet, Mexico, and tribes
segments.summary: The compact measured 16.4 million acre feet, split into 7.5 million per basin with the rest for Mexico. Tribes were left to fend for themselves in court. The upper basin must deliver 75 million acre feet over ten years.

segments.title: Law of the River and Boulder Canyon Project Act
segments.summary: The Law of the River is the body of compacts, court decisions and contracts. The 1928 Boulder Canyon Project Act ratified the compact and apportioned lower basin water among Arizona, California and Nevada. Arizona did not sign until 1944.

segments.title: Upper basin apportionment and Arizona v. California
segments.summary: The upper basin was apportioned in 1948 by percentage. Arizona v. California in 1963 split surplus water between Arizona and California and included reservations. A 1964 decree addressed tributary water.

segments.title: 1968 Colorado River Basin Project Act and Central Arizona Project
segments.summary: The 1968 act green-lit projects and gave California rights to surplus reserves in shortages. It created the Central Arizona Project, which supplied Phoenix and Tucson. The 1973 Endangered Species Act and 1974 salinity control act for Mexico are also noted.

segments.title: Drought begins and the 2019 contingency plan
segments.summary: A drought from 2000 to 2023 led basin states to coordinate reservoir releases. The 2019 Drought Contingency Plan followed.

segments.title: Flawed flow estimate and LaRue study
segments.summary: The 16.4 million acre feet figure came from a single Yuma study, though the LaRue survey gave a lower estimate that was set aside. Scientists say the states have overdrawn about a million acre feet a year.

segments.title: Declining flow, snowmelt, and agriculture
segments.summary: The river now produces about 13 million acre feet a year, and about 70 percent of its flow is snowmelt from the Rockies. Agriculture uses most of the water, mainly alfalfa and hay for cattle. The 1877 Desert Land Act and corporate land grabs are discussed.

segments.title: Dead pool risk and hydropower at Glen Canyon Dam
segments.summary: Lake Powell could fall so low that Glen Canyon Dam turbines stop and water cannot pass the penstocks, cutting off downstream supply.

segments.title: 2024 proposals, February 2026 deadline, and federal report
segments.summary: Lower basin states proposed shared cuts while the upper basin refused cuts. The February 13, 2026 deadline passed. In January 2026 the federal government released a 1,600-page report with options, and prior appropriation would likely apply. California is considering desalination.

segments.title: Listener mail: capri pants
segments.summary: Listener Vicky Read writes about the name for clam digger or capri pants, and recalls Mary Tyler Moore's capri pants on The Dick Van Dyke Show.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts thank the listener and give contact information and show credits.
